newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels hint at new talks in Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Rebels hint at new talks in Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's home in Peru said on Saturday they hoped talks with the government could resume but a gulf of mistrust still kept both sides apart.
With negotiations at an impasse, the rebels and President Alberto Fujimori both made bland statements of their wish to resume talks to end the siege, which has kept Peru on edge since Dec. 17.
But rebel charges that Fujimori's forces were building a secret tunnel with which to take the residence by storm while claiming to negotiate in good faith continued to poison the atmosphere.
A rebel spokeswoman said they had heard strange noises for days underneath the building in a posh Lima neighbourhood.

"We heard noises, not just for a moment but for several days. (At first) we didn't want to go public with this, we waited to find out for sure," said the guerrilla who identified herself only as Comrade Micaela in a walky-talky interview with Reuters.
"We are not frightened by this," she added defiantly.

The rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), demanding the release of hundreds of their captured comrades from jail, broke off talks on Thursday after angrily accusing the government of planning to overrun the residence via secret tunnels.
But suggesting a softer line, the guerrillas said on Saturday they were "evaluating" the situation and awaiting the arrival of a mediation group known as the guarantors' commission.
"We hope so," said Micaela, when asked in the radio interview about whether talks could resume.
"We are evaluating things and awaiting the guarantors' commission ... We're in constant evaluation," said guerrilla second-in-command Rolly Rojas in the same interview.
One member of the three-man commission, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, was later seen walking into the besieged residence with a folder in his hand. A Japanese doctor followed.

Fujimori said in a statement on Friday he hoped to resume talks to prevent bloodshed but that all talks were off if the rebels in any way harmed their hostages, including the president's brother Pedro, two cabinet ministers and top Japanese businessmen.
Police loudspeakers blasted traditional Latin American songs early on Saturday at the besieged residence while heavy fog rolled in off the Pacific.

Micaela, one of two teenage girls among the rebels, issued the MRTA's salute to International Women's Day with a furious speech in defence of "outcast and exploited women who fight day after day with their children against (Fujimori's) brutal economic policies."
"As women, we are fighting for a just cause. We want to liberate all our comrades who are being held prisoner. We will keep resisting until the end," she said.

Fujimori, a divorced father of four, paid his own tribute to International Women's Day by speaking to a neighbourhood mothers' organisation in a shantytown. Joking and looking in good spirits, he dodged questions about the alleged tunnel.

Fujimori's popularity has recovered from the spill it took when the siege began. A poll published on Saturday in a local newspaper but taken before the talks were broken off showed Fujimori's popularity rose some in February.
Datum Internacional's survey of 402 Lima residents said Fujimori's popularity rose to 47 percent last month from 43 percent in January, newspaper El Comercio said.

In Tokyo, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Saturday urged the Peruvian government and MRTA to resume talks to end the siege. "There is no benefit for either side in (the talks) remaining suspended," Hashimoto told reporters.
